name: The Argyle Street Ash

location.address: Outside 1223 Argyle Street (Franklin Terrace), Finnieston, Glasgow, Scotland

access: Free. Stands on Argyle Street itself, the only tree on the street, in the small front garden strip of a tenement building at Franklin Terrace; visible and reachable from the public pavement, no entry needed.
transport: Kelvinhall or Exhibition Centre subway/rail stations, both under 10 minutes' walk
verify_notes: UK Tree of the Year 2025 winner and UK's nominee for European Tree of the Year 2026 (12th place, 536 points). Wikipedia (citing James Cowan's 1951 'From Glasgow's Treasure Chest' and Alan Taylor's 'Glasgow: The Autobiography') gives the fuller, independently-sourced history: an ash seed was accidentally transplanted in the 1850s along with primrose roots brought back from holiday by residents of the newly-built tenement; already 75 feet (23m) tall by 1951, taller than the tenement itself. Was the first tree in Glasgow to receive a Tree Preservation Order. Only mildly affected by ash dieback (retains over 75% canopy), which Wikipedia attributes to its isolation (100m+ from the nearest ash) and urban microclimate (heat from adjacent buildings, paved surfaces reducing humidity, leaf litter swept away). Recent photo dated September 2024 on Wikipedia confirms it is alive and standing. Age: contest states 175 years (~1850s planting, consistent with Wikipedia's account); treat as a source-based estimate rather than a precise figure since the exact planting year is not recorded. No girth figure found in either source. Nominated by David Treanor, a local arborist who manages the tree. Fits the nearby Glasgow page (gla_002, the Suffragette Oak) well: same city, 0.71km away, a genuinely distinct urban specimen with a strong, well-documented human story.

name: The Plane Tree of Jászai Mari Square

location.address: Jászai Mari tér, District XIII, Budapest, Hungary
location.neighbourhood: Jászai Mari tér, District XIII (Ujlipotvaros/Angyalfold border), Budapest

access: Free. Stands in the middle of Jászai Mari tér, a well-tended public square/park at the Pest end of Margit Bridge, open at all times.
transport: Jászai Mari tér tram/bus stop (trams 4/6), right beside the square
verify_notes: Hungary's 2016 national 'Tree of the Year' (Ökotárs Alapítvány contest), 13th at the 2017 European final with 5132 votes. pestbuda.hu (2016), citing the contest's own application materials, says the tree was almost certainly planted in the late 1930s when the square was still called Rudolf ter, making it roughly 80-90 years old at that time (so about 90-100 today by extension, though nobody has re-measured since; kept the estimate closer to the sourced 2016 figure rather than extrapolating further). Girth 250cm and height 25m per pestbuda.hu, describing it as one of the last individuals of Budapest's 'plane tree era' of street planting. Survived WW2 fighting nearby (the Margit Bridge was blown up close by in 1944-45) as a sapling. Local literary connection: poet Miklos Radnoti's widow 'Fifi neni' watched it for decades from a nearby flat; writers Gyorgy Faludy, Margit Kovacs and Pal Rez also lived beside the square. Confirmed still standing and referred to as a living local landmark in welovebudapest.com's August 2024 piece on Budapest's historic plane trees. Species: sources just say 'platan' (plane); exact taxon (Platanus x acerifolia vs orientalis) not stated by any source, so kept at genus level rather than assuming the canonical London Plane label. Location is the contest's rounded park-level GPS (three decimal places, ~100m precision); no source pins the exact trunk within the square, so precision is approximate rather than confirmed. Fits Budapest (nearest published bud_010, 1.26km) well: a genuinely distinct, well-documented specimen in a public square, not a duplicate of anything already on the page.

name: The Lovers' Banyan Tree

location.address: Quinta das Lágrimas gardens, Rua António Augusto Gonçalves, Santa Clara, Coimbra, Portugal

access: Paid entry. Stands inside the Quinta das Lágrimas gardens, a historic estate and hotel grounds with a small public admission fee (reports of around 1 euro for the adjoining Fontes dos Lagrimas fountain area; the wider gardens charge a modest ticket too); open daily to visitors, not restricted to hotel guests.
transport: About a 20-25 minute walk south of central Coimbra (Santa Clara side of the Mondego); local buses serve the Quinta das Lágrimas stop
verify_notes: 2nd place, European Tree of the Year 2025, with 43,427 votes, nominated by the Fundação Inês de Castro. Stands beside the Fontanario/Fountain of Lovers in the Quinta das Lágrimas gardens, the traditional setting of the 14th-century legend of Pedro I of Portugal and Inês de Castro. Contest page says it was planted in the 19th century by an aristocratic tree collector through a seed exchange with the Sydney Botanic Garden; a WebSearch summary attributed this specifically to 'Miguel Osorio Cabral' but that name could not be confirmed on any page actually fetched, so it is left out of the record per the search-summary-is-a-lead-never-a-source rule; the planting story itself is corroborated across multiple press pieces reporting on the 2025 award. Known locally for its huge trunk, buttress roots and wide aerial-root canopy typical of Moreton Bay figs, and for being one of the most-photographed individual trees in Portugal. No girth or height figure was found on any page actually fetched (a couple of secondary listicles quoted numbers but none were confirmed on the source itself, so left out). Location is the contest's published GPS, which lands inside the gardens near the fountain area but is not a tree-level survey point, so kept as approximate rather than confirmed; the tree is unmistakable on site (an aristocratic garden's single huge fig by a named fountain), so a future pass with a park map or satellite check of the garden could likely upgrade this. Genuinely distinct from Coimbra's existing page (cbr_001, the Bunya Pine of the Arcos do Jardim, 1.63km away): different species, different garden, no overlap.

name: The Peace Tree of Woodvale Park

location.address: Woodvale Park, Woodvale Road, Belfast, Northern Ireland, UK

access: Free. Stands in Woodvale Park, a Belfast City Council public park with a Green Flag Award; the park opens at 7:30am daily. Surrounded by a protective railing installed by the council, but visible and reachable on foot within the park.
transport: On Woodvale Road; served by Belfast Metro bus routes into the Shankill/Woodvale area, roughly 25-30 minutes' walk or a short bus ride from the city centre
verify_notes: Voted Northern Ireland's Tree of the Year 2015 (Woodland Trust NI contest, nominated jointly by historian Bobby Foster and Sam Coulter), then 13th at the 2016 European final with 628 votes. Planted on Empire Day (24 May) 1919 in honour of local men who did not return from the First World War; became a focal point for veterans, was then largely forgotten, and was rediscovered in 2006 (90th anniversary of the Somme) per the contest page. Wikipedia's Woodvale Park article independently confirms the tree, its 1919 planting and its continued presence in the park, and that a European War Memorial (unveiled 2014) now stands beside it, remembering German, French, Belgian and British dead alike. Age: contest gives 96 years as of 2016, so roughly 105-110 today by extension from the same 1919 planting date; this is arithmetic on a source-documented year, not a fresh estimate. No girth or height recorded anywhere found. Coordinates are the contest's GPS to the nearest few seconds, which lands inside the park but reads as a rounded figure (exactly 54.61 latitude) rather than a raw on-site reading, so kept approximate rather than confirmed; the park is not large and the tree is railed off and locally famous, so it should be easy for a future pass or a park map to pin exactly. Genuinely distinct from the existing Belfast page (bfs_002, the Grass Tree of the Palm House, 3.74km away): different park, different story, no overlap. A good fit for Belfast's page: free, public, well-documented, one clear thing to stand at.
